summary: Specifies extensions to the Host Identity Protocol for NAT traversal, using the ICE methodology to find a working path between two hosts and standard techniques to relay when needed. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: HIP gives devices names that stay with them. This document helps such devices reach each other even when home routers hide them, by trying different paths until one works.

questions: how does hip work through nat
what is a hip relay server
how do ice connectivity checks work
subtitle: Extensions to help HIP work through network address translators.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) normally does not work through NATs because it runs directly over IP. Devices behind NATs cannot reach each other with HIP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds UDP encapsulation to carry HIP control packets and data through NATs, plus the ICE methodology to discover a working path between hosts, and support for relay servers to bootstrap connections.
tldr.outcome: HIP-enabled hosts behind NATs can now establish direct connections by trying multiple address pairs, or fall back to relaying traffic when needed.

today: RFC 5770 is Experimental. It defines how HIP implementations can traverse NATs using ICE and relay servers, allowing HIP hosts behind NATs to find each other.

sections.title: Why HIP Needs NAT Traversal
sections.content:
HIP was designed to run directly over IPv4 or IPv6. It gives every host a stable identity, called a Host Identity Tag (HIT), that stays with the host even when its network address changes. This is powerful for mobility and multihoming, but it has a problem: the protocol does not understand Network Address Translators (NATs).

A NAT is a middlebox that sits between a private network and the public Internet. It rewrites IP addresses in packets so that hosts on the private side can communicate outside. HIP packets sent directly over IP confuse NATs because the NATs do not know how to rewrite HIP headers. If both hosts are behind NATs, they cannot reach each other with bare HIP. This RFC extends HIP so it can work in these environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Your home router hides your computer from the Internet and gives you a secret address only the router knows. HIP does not like that hiding. This document teaches HIP to ask the router nicely and find a way through.

sections.title: The NAT Traversal Approach
sections.content:
The extensions use three main techniques. First, they wrap HIP and ESP packets in UDP, which most NATs forward without complaint. Second, they adopt the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) method from Session Initiation Protocol to test many possible address pairs between the two hosts and find one that works. Third, they define a HIP relay server that can forward control packets to hosts behind NATs when a direct path fails.

The hosts exchange lists of candidate addresses during the HIP base exchange. These candidates include the host's own local address (a host candidate), the public address the host sees when it queries a STUN server or HIP relay (a server reflexive candidate), and an address provided by a TURN relay (a relayed candidate). The hosts then try these address pairs in order of preference until one works. If all fail, they fall back to relaying through the TURN server.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides try calling each other from different phone numbers until one works. If none work, they use a answering service to relay calls between them.

sections.title: Two Modes of NAT Traversal
sections.content:
The RFC defines two NAT traversal modes. The first, UDP-ENCAPSULATION, is simple: wrap HIP and ESP packets in UDP and send them directly. This mode assumes the host knows it can reach the other side without ICE checks. It is used when one host is not behind a NAT, or when the network is simple enough that the path works without testing.

The second mode, ICE-STUN-UDP, performs full ICE connectivity checks using STUN messages to probe each address pair. This is more robust and works in complex NAT topologies. The two hosts negotiate which mode to use during the HIP base exchange. They also negotiate a transaction pacing value, which is the minimum time between connectivity checks, to avoid overwhelming the NATs with test traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either just try calling directly, or carefully test each phone number to see which ones work. The two sides agree beforehand on which approach to use.

sections.title: Relay Servers Bootstrap Connections
sections.content:
A HIP relay server is a middlebox that forwards HIP control packets between an Initiator and a Responder. Unlike the earlier HIP rendezvous server, which only forwarded the first I1 packet, a relay server forwards all control packets of the base exchange. This is essential for NAT traversal because the Initiator must register with the relay and then use it to send I2 and I1 packets to the Responder. The relay server does not handle data traffic; that uses TURN relays if needed.

When a host registers with a relay, the relay learns the host's public transport address and sends it back in a REG_FROM parameter. The host then includes this address as a server reflexive candidate. This way, the other side knows where to reach the host.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay server is like an answering service that saves your public phone number and gives it to callers so they can find you.

sections.title: Base Exchange and Connectivity Checks
sections.content: The base exchange via a relay works as follows. The Initiator sends an I1 over UDP to the relay, which appends a RELAY_FROM parameter containing the Initiator's observed address and forwards it to the Responder. The Responder replies with R1, which includes RELAY_TO telling the Initiator's address and NAT_TRAVERSAL_MODE listing supported modes. The Initiator then sends I2 with its list of candidate addresses (the ICE offer) and the selected mode. The Responder replies with R2 and its own candidates (the ICE answer). After the base exchange, if ICE mode was selected, the hosts perform connectivity checks using STUN Binding requests until they find a working pair. They use that pair for ESP data traffic and also send periodic NAT keepalives to prevent NAT state from timing out.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides exchange messages through the relay, telling each other all their possible addresses. Then they test the pairs one by one until they find one that works, and they send regular ping messages to keep the connection fresh.
